posts.title: Allergen Labelling in India: What to Declare and How
posts.description: Review allergens from the complete formula, including compound ingredients and supplier carriers, and prepare the required declaration
posts.lede: Review allergens from the complete formula, including compound ingredients and supplier carriers, and prepare the required declaration. A precautionary cross-contact statement serves a different purpose from declaring an allergen intentionally present. Neither statement replaces controls in the facility.
posts.body:
Identify the listed allergen sources

The regulations cover specified gluten-containing cereals, crustaceans, milk, egg, fish, peanuts and tree nuts, soybeans and sulphites at 10 mg/kg or more. Check the exact wording and exemptions for the product rather than expanding or narrowing the list from memory. Read regulation 5 allergen provisions.

Trace every component

Review fillings, seasoning, enzyme preparations, flavours and premixes as well as major ingredients. Supplier changes can affect the assessment without changing the marketing name. Record the allergen source and where it enters the formula, and resolve incomplete specifications before approving an absence claim.

Separate presence from cross-contact

An intentional milk ingredient requires the relevant presence declaration. Possible cross-contact from shared equipment is a separate risk assessment for precautionary wording. A generic may-contain line should not conceal a known ingredient or substitute for cleaning, segregation and supplier controls.

Assess special exemptions precisely

The regulations contain specified exemptions, including treatment of raw agricultural commodities and particular derived products. Apply them only where the product fits the provision. A refined ingredient or a product that is itself an allergen requires a documented reading of the applicable text, not a broad all-natural exemption.

Control claims and artwork changes

Before saying allergen-free or gluten-free, assess the applicable claim criteria and product evidence. Reconcile the allergen statement with the ingredient list and all sales channels. Keep supplier approvals, cleaning assessments and artwork versions so a change can be traced. Build a claim evidence file.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A snack uses a seasoning whose specification includes milk powder. The ingredient team identifies intentional milk presence, while the facility separately assesses possible nut cross-contact from a shared line. The two decisions use different evidence and are not combined into an indiscriminate may-contain-all statement.

Your practical checklist

  • Review the complete formula and components.
  • Map listed allergens to their sources.
  • Check sulphite concentration where relevant.
  • Assess cross-contact controls separately.
  • Apply exemptions only to matching facts.
  • Reconcile labels and any absence claims.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Allergen Declaration Review service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

faq.q: Can may-contain replace an intentional-allergen statement?
faq.a: No. Intentional presence and cross-contact require separate assessments.

faq.q: Do premix allergens count?
faq.a: Yes. Review their contribution to the finished product.

faq.q: What is the sulphite threshold?
faq.a: The cited rule lists sulphites at 10 mg/kg or more.

faq.q: Can I say gluten-free without evidence?
faq.a: Review the applicable claim criterion, formula and supporting product evidence.

faq.q: Do supplier changes need an allergen review?
faq.a: Yes. Component changes may alter the assessment even when the product name stays the same.

posts.title: How to Make a Nutrition Information Table for Your Label
posts.description: Build the nutrition table from reliable product data on the reporting basis required for the food
posts.lede: Build the nutrition table from reliable product data on the reporting basis required for the food. Check the recipe version, serving size, units and applicable RDA contribution. A laboratory report cannot simply be pasted onto a label without interpreting its basis and scope.
posts.body:
Define the reporting basis

The general provisions address information per 100 g, 100 ml or single-consumption pack, together with per-serve percentage contribution to the specified reference requirements. Establish whether the product is reported as sold or under a relevant preparation instruction and category rule. Read nutrition requirements.

Identify the required nutrients

Assess energy, protein, carbohydrate, total and added sugars, fat-related declarations and sodium under the applicable provisions. Saturated fat, trans fat and cholesterol have specific conditions. Claimed nutrients and specialised categories can add requirements. Do not delete a field merely because a generic template omits it.

Prepare the calculation file

Use the actual recipe and appropriate analysis or justified data. Record units, moisture basis, preparation instructions and the difference between total and added sugars. A total-sugar test alone does not determine added sugar from the manufacturing formula. Keep supplier composition and recipe records available.

Calculate serving information transparently

For a hypothetical food with 400 kcal per 100 g, a 25 g serving supplies 100 kcal. On a 2000 kcal adult reference basis, that represents 5% of daily energy. This arithmetic example illustrates scaling only; other nutrients use their own prescribed reference values and conditions.

Check exceptions and future changes

Apply nutrition exemptions only where the product fits the rule, remembering that claims can affect the position. The March 2026 amendment includes changes with a 1 July 2027 effective date. Record current and future versions separately rather than treating every notified amendment as immediately operative. Read the effective date.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A beverage report states sodium in mg per 100 ml, but artwork labels the same number as grams per serving. The review converts units and serving quantities, then rechecks the RDA column. The analytical value was correct; the label interpretation was not.

Your practical checklist

  • Confirm recipe and reporting basis.
  • Identify required and claimed nutrients.
  • Review analytical and formulation evidence.
  • Check units and serving conversions.
  • Use the correct nutrient-specific reference values.
  • Verify exemptions and effective dates.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Nutrition Information Review service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

faq.q: Can I copy another product’s panel?
faq.a: No. Nutrition information must reflect your actual product and applicable requirements.

faq.q: Does a test report prove added sugar?
faq.a: Not by itself. Added-sugar assessment also depends on formulation and source data.

faq.q: Is sodium the same as salt?
faq.a: No. Use the prescribed declaration and any justified conversion carefully.

faq.q: Can I omit all nutrition for a small pack?
faq.a: Assess the specific exemption and conditions; pack size alone is not a complete answer.

faq.q: When do the cited March 2026 changes apply?
faq.a: The notification specifies 1 July 2027 for its provisions.

posts.title: Veg and Non-Veg Logo Rules (Size, Colour, Placement)
posts.description: The vegetarian symbol uses a green circle within a green outlined square; the current non-vegetarian symbol uses a brown triangle within a brown outlined square
posts.lede: The vegetarian symbol uses a green circle within a green outlined square; the current non-vegetarian symbol uses a brown triangle within a brown outlined square. Assess the complete product before choosing the symbol, then check the prescribed size and front-of-pack placement.
posts.body:
Determine the product’s status

Review ingredients, additives, processing sources and supplier specifications. Milk-derived ingredients do not by themselves make a food non-vegetarian under the general definition, while egg and relevant animal-origin materials need assessment. A plant-based marketing name is insufficient evidence for every input.

Use the current symbols

The non-vegetarian triangle is important: an old brown-circle artwork is not the current prescribed design. This guide’s original review illustration does not reproduce official marks. Obtain the correct authorised symbol specification for production artwork. Read the symbol provisions.

Apply the principal-display-panel size table

PDP area in cm²Veg circle diameter, mmNon-veg triangle side, mmSurrounding square side, mm
Up to 10032.56
Above 100 to 50043.58
Above 500 to 25006512
Above 25008716

These are the minimum dimensions in the cited table. Measure the actual principal display panel rather than using the total area of an unrelated dieline.

Review placement and exceptions

The symbol is to be prominent against a contrasting background on the principal display panel, close to the name or brand on the front. Specified product exemptions must be checked against the regulation. Applicable promotional material also needs a declaration assessment, not just the physical package.

Distinguish vegetarian from vegan

A vegetarian mark does not establish vegan compliance. Milk, honey and other sources relevant to vegan rules require a separate product and process review, and the vegan logo has an endorsement framework. Read organic and vegan endorsement guidance.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A small pouch’s designer reduces both the symbol and square to fit a crowded corner. The team measures the PDP, checks the prescribed dimensions and moves other copy instead. It also verifies the flavour supplier’s source information before confirming the product status.

  • Use the current circle or triangle design.
  • Measure the principal display panel.
  • Apply minimum symbol and square dimensions.
  • Check placement, contrast and exceptions.
  • Assess vegan statements separately.

posts.title: FSSAI Logo and Licence Number on the Label: Rules
posts.description: A food label must carry the applicable FSSAI logo and licence-number declarations for the responsible businesses
posts.lede: A food label must carry the applicable FSSAI logo and licence-number declarations for the responsible businesses. The brand owner and a different manufacturer, marketer, packer or bottler can require separate details. The number is a business identifier, not an endorsement of the product’s claims.
posts.body:
Map the responsible businesses

Identify the brand owner, manufacturing site, packer, marketer and importer where relevant. Match each role to the actual agreement, certificate and product. Do not choose one number merely because the contract factory has supplied a ready-made label.

Read the declaration requirements

The Labelling and Display regulations address the brand-owner licence number and the applicable number where a different business performs listed roles. Assess the exact arrangement and declaration wording together. Read the business and licence declarations.

Verify the numbers and addresses

Compare each issued certificate with the artwork and invoice file. Check the premises and status, and resolve inconsistent spelling or manufacturing-site information. A head-office number does not automatically explain the site where a product is made. Use the verification guide.

Use the official logo appropriately

Obtain the prescribed artwork and review its presentation and legibility. Avoid changing the logo into a promotional badge or implying that FSSAI has approved a health benefit. The original illustrations supplied with this collection deliberately use educational diagrams rather than official-looking certification artwork.

Control changes and print versions

A new factory, operator or product arrangement can affect the declarations. Link the approved label to current certificates and record the decision. For imported food, review importer information and the permitted correction framework separately; a domestic label decision does not establish port-sticker permissions.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A private-label snack identifies the brand owner and contract factory as different businesses. The team checks the applicable number and address declarations for both roles and verifies the manufacturing premises. It avoids printing a single unexplained number supplied in a design template.

Your practical checklist

  • Map brand owner and other responsible roles.
  • Collect current issued certificates.
  • Verify numbers, status and premises.
  • Apply the exact declaration requirements.
  • Use prescribed logo artwork legibly.
  • Recheck after factory or operator changes.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Basic Artwork Review service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

faq.q: Can I print the manufacturer’s number only?
faq.a: Assess the applicable brand-owner and other responsible-business declarations.

faq.q: Does the logo mean FSSAI approves my claim?
faq.a: No. Claims and product compliance require their own assessment.

faq.q: Can I use another business’s number?
faq.a: Only the actual applicable responsible businesses and authorisations should be declared.

faq.q: Do imported packs need importer information?
faq.a: Yes. Assess the import-specific declarations and applicable rules.

faq.q: Should factory changes trigger label review?
faq.a: Yes. Responsible-business information may need revision.

posts.title: Legal Metrology on Food Packs: Net Quantity, MRP and Consumer Care
posts.description: For retail food packs, review Legal Metrology declarations alongside FSSAI information
posts.lede: For retail food packs, review Legal Metrology declarations alongside FSSAI information. Net quantity, MRP inclusive of taxes, consumer-care details and applicable unit sale price are distinct tasks. Accurate nutrition and ingredients do not make the commercial declarations complete.
posts.body:
Establish the package and sale type

Identify the actual prepacked commodity, retail unit, multipack, wholesale or institutional arrangement and applicable exemptions. A large carton is not automatically exempt, and a business-to-business invoice does not alone establish institutional-consumer treatment.

Check the commercial declaration set

The Department of Consumer Affairs overview identifies relevant manufacturer/packer/importer information, common or generic name, net quantity, date-related information, MRP including taxes, consumer-care details and unit sale price. Apply the actual rules to the product and pack. Official declaration overview.

Control quantity and price calculations

Use the appropriate standard units and distinguish net food quantity from packaging weight. Match the declaration to filling and quantity-control records. Where unit sale price applies, calculate it on the prescribed basis and reconcile it with the displayed MRP and quantity; do not create a decorative comparison price.

Read current amendments before approving wording

The official rules directory includes several 2026 amendments. Older compilations remain useful for structure but should not be treated as the complete current law. Check the relevant amendment, effective date and commodity scope rather than assuming every change applies to every food. Current rules and amendments.

Review the physical and online presentation

Check legibility, location and accurate consumer-care channels. Review online declaration duties for the sale model. MRP alterations or stickers require their own rule and direction assessment; a tax change does not give an unlimited right to rewrite prices. Coordinate the review with FSSAI date and business declarations.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A brand launches a 200 g pack using the MRP and unit-price artwork from its 250 g version. The team recalculates the applicable price presentation and checks net-quantity controls. The product formula is unchanged, but the commercial declaration file must still be updated.

Your practical checklist

  • Identify retail and other package formats.
  • Check applicable declarations and exemptions.
  • Verify net quantity and standard units.
  • Reconcile MRP, taxes and unit sale price.
  • Review current amendments and dates.
  • Check physical and online consumer information.

posts.keyword: best before vs expiry date fssai
posts.title: Date Marking: Best Before vs Use By vs Expiry
posts.description: Best-before concerns the period of expected quality, while expiry or use-by marks the end of the stated period for the product under its storage conditions
posts.lede: Best-before concerns the period of expected quality, while expiry or use-by marks the end of the stated period for the product under its storage conditions. Current Indian food-labelling rules require a date-marking assessment that includes manufacture or packing and expiry/use-by; best-before may be additional.
posts.body:
Read the terms in context

A date statement depends on the food, storage conditions and validated shelf life. Do not replace one expression with another solely to make a product seem longer lasting. The regulations define and use the terms differently. Read date-marking requirements.

Check required dates and exceptions

The general provision addresses manufacture or packing and expiry/use-by, with best-before as optional additional information. Specific exemptions and short-life or category provisions must be checked precisely. A single best-before line copied from a foreign pack is not a complete current Indian assessment.

Support the shelf-life decision

Use appropriate product, process, packaging and storage evidence. Consider relevant microbiological, chemical and sensory risks and whether the product changes after opening. A raw-material certificate or competitor’s date does not establish finished-product shelf life.

Make the code usable

Plan the actual location, contrast and date format, including variable printing. Link the batch or lot to production and distribution records. Check that coding survives normal handling and is not hidden by a fold, cap or secondary label. Printed storage instructions should match the evidence supporting the dates.

Apply the dates through the supply chain

Set receiving, stock rotation, dispatch and marketplace controls so the correct product reaches customers with suitable remaining life. Imported food has a separate remaining-shelf-life clearance assessment. Read import-rejection risks. Do not equate an internal quality review after best-before with permission to sell food beyond its expiry/use-by position.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A chilled dessert’s artwork says store refrigerated, while dispatch routinely uses unvalidated ambient transport. The date review identifies that the storage assumption does not match the delivery process. Changing the printed month cannot fix the handling gap.

Your practical checklist

  • Identify applicable required date statements.
  • Check category-specific exemptions.
  • Support shelf life for the actual food and pack.
  • Match storage and use instructions to evidence.
  • Verify legible batch and date coding.
  • Control receiving, dispatch and remaining life.

faq.q: Is best-before identical to expiry?
faq.a: No. They have different regulatory meanings and purposes.

faq.q: Can I use only best-before on every pack?
faq.a: No. Assess current manufacture/packing and expiry/use-by requirements and exceptions.

faq.q: Can I copy a competitor’s shelf life?
faq.a: No. Support the decision for your own product, process and packaging.

faq.q: Does refrigeration wording matter?
faq.a: Yes. Date validity depends on the stated storage conditions being appropriate.

faq.q: Are imports checked for remaining shelf life?
faq.a: Yes. Assess the applicable import provision separately.

posts.title: Front-of-Pack Labelling in India: Where Things Stand
posts.description: Review current mandatory front-of-pack information separately from the proposed Indian Nutrition Rating system
posts.lede: Review current mandatory front-of-pack information separately from the proposed Indian Nutrition Rating system. The September 2022 INR document is a draft. This research did not establish an operative blanket INR star-rating mandate as of 2 October 2026; verify later final notifications before changing artwork.
posts.body:
Understand what front-of-pack means

The front is where consumers encounter product identity and prominent claims. Existing rules already address declarations such as applicable vegetarian/non-vegetarian symbols and their placement. Nutrition information and specialised warnings have their own requirements. Front-of-pack is not synonymous with a voluntary design style.

What the INR draft proposed

The 2022 draft proposes an interpretive nutrition-rating system using relevant negative and positive factors and a star presentation. Its formula, exceptions and illustrations belong to that proposal. Do not use the draft logo as evidence that a product has been officially rated or that the system is mandatory. Read the draft notification.

Check legal status, scope and timing

For any later development, identify the final Gazette text, amendments, effective date, transition arrangements and product exemptions. A consultation, scientific discussion or news report is insufficient to establish an operative duty. Check the official notification register together with the current labelling rules. Official notifications.

What brands can prepare now

Keep reliable nutrient data, controlled recipes and adequate design space for required information. Review existing front claims against the Advertising and Claims rules. These tasks support current compliance and make future adaptation easier without printing a speculative rating.

Avoid confusing separate 2026 changes

The March 2026 labelling amendment cited in this collection has its own scope and July 2027 effective date. It should not be presented as a final INR mandate. Maintain a change register that separates proposals, final future requirements and requirements already effective.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A cereal brand asks a designer to add five stars after reading a news article. The team finds only the cited draft basis, retains current mandatory declarations and reviews its actual nutrition claims. It waits for an established legal basis before presenting any official-style rating.

Your practical checklist

  • Check existing front-of-pack duties.
  • Identify whether a rating document is draft or final.
  • Verify scope, effective date and exemptions.
  • Maintain reliable nutrient data.
  • Review current claims independently.
  • Record later notification checks before print.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Front-of-Pack Review service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

headings.text: Check legal status, scope and timing

faq.a: The cited document is a draft notification.

faq.q: Can I print an official-looking rating now?
faq.a: Establish the operative basis and authorised use before doing so.

faq.q: Do current front declarations still apply?
faq.a: Yes. Existing applicable labelling requirements remain separate.

faq.q: Does every 2026 label amendment concern INR?
faq.a: No. Read the actual scope and effective date of each notification.

faq.q: How should I track future changes?
faq.a: Use the official register and retain the final text, applicability assessment and implementation date.

posts.title: Label Rules for Small Packs and Multipacks
posts.description: Small packs and multipacks need a format-specific review of exemptions and outer-pack declarations
posts.lede: Small packs and multipacks need a format-specific review of exemptions and outer-pack declarations. Limited space does not create a general right to omit mandatory information. Assess each selling unit and the conditions of any exemption before simplifying the artwork.
posts.body:
Identify every layer sold to customers

Map the inner unit, bundle, outer wrapper and transport carton. Record which units may be sold separately. A promotional bundle of independently sold sachets is different from a multipack whose inner units are not individual retail units.

Measure the relevant area

Use the actual package dimensions and applicable surface-area or principal-display-panel definition. These measurements can serve different provisions; do not use one number interchangeably for every size rule. Keep the dieline and measurement calculation in the review file.

Read each exemption independently

Labelling rules contain specified small-pack provisions and conditions for information on the outer package. Check the exact declaration being considered, the size threshold and any statement or condition required. An ingredient-list exemption does not automatically remove allergen, date, symbol or commercial duties. Read small-pack provisions.

Review multipack information and Legal Metrology

Check the quantity and unit structure, product names, dates, business information and applicable price declarations. Where units differ, do not describe the bundle as if every item has identical composition or shelf life. Assess retail, wholesale and institutional treatment against the actual sale. Read the current metrology rules.

Proof the real pack

Check whether seals, folds and overwrap hide declarations. Review a realistic printed sample at actual size, including variable codes. If legibility cannot be achieved, reconsider pack design and information architecture rather than shrinking all copy until it becomes unusable.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A brand bundles four snack sachets but allows shops to sell them individually. The review does not assume outer-wrapper information will always reach the buyer. It assesses the individual retail units and bundle separately before relying on any small-pack provision.

Your practical checklist

  • Map retail units and outer layers.
  • Record separate-sale arrangements.
  • Measure the correct relevant areas.
  • Check each exemption and condition.
  • Review bundle quantity, dates and price.
  • Inspect the finished actual-size pack.

Download this preparation checklist

faq.q: Does a small pack avoid all declarations?
faq.a: No. Exemptions are specific and conditional.

faq.q: Can the outer carton carry everything?
faq.a: Only where the applicable provision and sale arrangement support that treatment.

faq.q: Does a multipack make inner units non-retail?
faq.a: Not automatically. Assess whether they are sold separately.

faq.q: Can I reduce symbol size freely?
faq.a: Apply the relevant prescribed dimensions and actual exemption, if any.

faq.q: Should I inspect a physical sample?
faq.a: Yes. It helps identify folds, seals and coding problems not obvious on screen.

posts.title: Pre-Print Checklist: What to Check Before Your Label Goes to the Printer
posts.description: Before printing, reconcile the final artwork with the approved recipe, reports, certificates and applicable label requirements
posts.lede: Before printing, reconcile the final artwork with the approved recipe, reports, certificates and applicable label requirements. Review the actual-size proof and variable coding. A design approval email should identify the exact file and unresolved conditions, not merely say looks good.
posts.body:
Freeze the source data

Confirm formula, ingredient specifications, allergen assessment, nutrition basis, shelf-life decision, responsible businesses and licence records. Record the version of each source. A last-minute ingredient substitution should reopen affected declarations even if the printer is already booked.

Review the declaration matrix

Check product identity, ingredients, additives, allergens, nutrition, symbols, business details, dates, quantity, price and consumer care as applicable. Review claims separately against their evidence. Use current operative requirements and effective dates. Food-labelling rules; claims criteria.

Inspect the production proof

Check dimensions, contrast, type size, colour, panel placement, folds, seams and material. Plan where the batch and dates will be printed and confirm that the production line can produce readable codes. A high-resolution screen view at 300% does not prove legibility on the finished pouch.

Control approval and printer handover

Assign a file identifier and preserve the reviewed PDF and production file. Record conditions such as variable data or pending certificate confirmation. Avoid sending unreviewed editable files after approving a different proof. Confirm the printer’s version matches the final approved reference.

Check the first printed output

Compare the first production samples with the approved proof before releasing the complete run. Record discrepancies and their disposition. Keep a sample and the decision record with the batch documentation so later complaints or changes can be investigated. Read multi-SKU control.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A designer sends a final PDF, then corrects an MRP in the editable source without regenerating the approved proof. The printer receives the wrong version. A file-identifier and final-proof check would have made the discrepancy visible before printing.

Your practical checklist

  • Freeze formula and supporting data versions.
  • Review every applicable declaration and claim.
  • Inspect actual-size artwork and coding areas.
  • Record the exact approved file and conditions.
  • Confirm printer handover versions.
  • Check and retain the first production sample.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Pre-Print Final Artwork Sign-Off service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

faq.q: Is design approval the same as regulatory review?
faq.a: No. Ensure the applicable content and evidence have been reviewed.

faq.q: Can the printer decide missing legal wording?
faq.a: Provide controlled, reviewed inputs rather than leaving regulatory decisions implicit.

faq.q: Should variable dates be in the proof?
faq.a: Show the coding location and expected format, and verify the production output.

faq.q: Can a last-minute formula change be ignored?
faq.a: No. Reassess the declarations and claims affected by it.

faq.q: What should sign-off identify?
faq.a: The exact file, reviewed scope, source versions and any unresolved conditions.

posts.title: Harmonising Labels Across a Product Range
posts.description: Harmonise a product range through controlled common rules and SKU-specific data
posts.lede: Harmonise a product range through controlled common rules and SKU-specific data. Shared layout can improve consistency, but ingredients, allergens, nutrition, dates and claims must remain linked to each actual product. A master template should make differences visible rather than conceal them.
posts.body:
Create a SKU source matrix

Record legal name, recipe version, supplier components, allergens, nutrition report, claim decision, pack sizes, manufacturing site and shelf-life basis for every SKU. Mark which fields are truly common and which require individual review. Keep the matrix connected to the artwork file identifiers.

Standardise legitimate shared elements

Agree placement, approved business wording, typography and information hierarchy where the rules and facts permit. Use the applicable Labelling and Display requirements and current commercial declarations as constraints. Consistency should follow reviewed requirements rather than an attractive but unsuitable house style. Read the labelling rules.

Protect SKU-specific declarations

A new flavour may introduce allergens, different additives or a changed nutrition profile. A different pack size can change serving, quantity, price or symbol-size questions. Do not duplicate the first approved label and assume the rest only need a colour and flavour-name change.

Control manufacturing and commercial variants

Where sites or responsible businesses differ, map the correct details to each version. Review local, export and imported presentations separately. Use a controlled variant register so overseas artwork or a discontinued factory version does not reach the domestic printer.

Make changes across the range deliberately

Define a change request describing the source update and affected SKUs. Recheck connected fields, approve the revised files and remove obsolete versions from shared folders. Keep evidence of which batches used each artwork. Follow the pre-print process.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A brand’s three granola flavours share a design, but one adds peanut butter and another changes the serving size. The source matrix identifies the separate allergen and nutrition decisions. The team keeps common layout rules while approving product-specific copy.

Your practical checklist

  • Build a complete SKU and source matrix.
  • Identify genuinely common elements.
  • Protect formula-specific declarations.
  • Map pack-size and site variants.
  • Use controlled file and batch references.
  • Apply changes to all affected versions.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Multi-SKU Artwork Harmonisation service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

headings.text: Make changes across the range deliberately

faq.q: Can all flavours use one ingredient list?
faq.a: Only if it accurately reflects each product; different formulas usually require distinct copy.

faq.q: Can nutrition values be shared automatically?
faq.a: No. Establish a justified basis for each actual product.

faq.q: Does pack size affect compliance?
faq.a: It can affect quantities, servings, price and presentation requirements.

faq.q: What is a useful master template?
faq.a: One that standardises valid common elements and clearly identifies SKU-specific fields.

faq.q: How do I prevent outdated files?
faq.a: Control version identifiers, approvals and printer access to the current release.

posts.title: Food Claims in India: What You Can Say on Packs, Websites and Ads
posts.description: Assess nutrition, health, natural and non-addition claims using FSSAI rules, worked examples and an evidence-file workflow for food brands.
posts.lede: A food claim must fit the product, the applicable conditions and the evidence behind it. Review the same message wherever customers see it: on the pack, the website, marketplace listings, advertising and promotional content.
posts.body:
What counts as a food claim?

The Advertising and Claims Regulations address consumer messages beyond the package. Claims can concern composition, nutritional properties, origin, processing or health; advertisements and marketing communications have a broad scope. Read the original regulations alongside amendments.

Begin with an inventory of what a customer would see or hear. Include words, pictures, comparisons, captions and spoken scripts. A small line beneath a large headline may affect the overall message, but it cannot be assumed to repair it.

Review the product title and brand presentation too. The useful question is what the entire communication tells a consumer about this food. Treat the answer as a hypothesis to assess against the product's facts, rather than focusing on one carefully chosen word.

Separate nutrition, non-addition and health claims

Proposed messagePrimary review question
“High protein” or “low fat”Does the product meet the applicable nutrient-content condition?
“No added sugar”Does the formulation and manufacturing process support non-addition?
A statement about a physiological benefitWhat claim type, evidence and conditions apply?
“Less sugar than…”Is the comparison valid, identifiable and properly presented?
“Natural” or “fresh”Do the conditions for the term fit the product and processing?

The categories are useful because each asks a different evidentiary question. A nutrient test, a recipe record and a scientific dossier perform different jobs. Decide what the claim asserts before choosing the evidence that might support it.

Give each proposed statement a unique entry in a claims register. Record the exact words, SKU, channel, intended audience and reviewer. Avoid approving a vague concept such as “health messaging” when the actual advertisement has not been written.

Common nutrition-claim criteria to verify

The current claims compendium provides the following selected conditions. They are screening references; assess the complete rule and product context before using a claim. Schedule I and general conditions.

ClaimSelected condition
Sugar freeSugars no more than 0.5 g per 100 g or 100 ml.
Low fatFat no more than 3 g/100 g for solids or 1.5 g/100 ml for liquids.
High/rich in proteinProtein at least 20% of RDA/100 g for solids; 10%/100 ml for liquids; or the specified alternatives of 10%/100 kcal or 20%/serving.

Protein needs an RDA-based assessment under the Indian conditions. Do not substitute a foreign percentage-of-energy criterion. Read the protein row in full.

Hypothetical calculation check

A beverage report shows 0.8 g sugars per 100 ml, while the copywriter uses “sugar free.” Comparing the value with the selected condition exposes a mismatch. Before changing the wording, verify that the report, units and formulation match the product being marketed.

Include a reasonable review margin in the development discussion. If the product is close to a claim boundary, ask the technical team how changes in formulation, ingredients and production could affect the result. The claim-review decision should reflect the evidence for the product that will actually be sold.

No added sugar is a formulation question

The non-addition conditions look beyond table sugar: sugars can come from components and ingredients used to replace added sugar. Naturally present sugars require the applicable accompanying statement when the claim is used. Review regulation 6.

Make a component-level ingredient map. For each supplier ingredient, identify what it contains and why it is used. Ask whether a sweetened component, syrup, fruit preparation or processing step changes the claim assessment. Resolve uncertain supplier descriptions before making a blanket statement.

Hypothetical formulation review

A recipe uses unsweetened oats and a fruit preparation whose component list has not been collected. The team should obtain that list and understand the ingredient's function before settling the claim. A purchase invoice saying “fruit mix” cannot establish the complete formulation.

Keep the assessment with the approved recipe version. If procurement later changes the ingredient, ask whether the approved non-addition wording remains supported. Supplier changes should reach the label and marketing reviewers before the product goes back into production.

Health claims need evidence matched to the actual assertion

The regulations distinguish health claims from nutrient-content statements and prohibit medicinal claims except where specifically permitted. Product-health claims have particular evidence requirements; a general paper about an ingredient is not automatically a basis for the finished product's claim. Review health and prohibited-claim provisions.

Write the proposed benefit in a complete sentence. Identify the product or constituent said to produce the benefit, the intended audience and the consumption conditions. Then ask the scientific reviewer whether the evidence addresses that proposition.

A study can be relevant yet leave important gaps. The studied ingredient may have a different specification; the dose may differ; the study population may not match the audience; or the outcome may be narrower than the headline. Document those differences rather than hiding them behind a long bibliography.

For a review dossier, create an evidence table with the study, tested material, use level, population, outcome and limitations. Keep the original paper or source reference. A marketing summary of the research should be checked against what the study actually reports.

When a claim or category requires a particular regulatory route, establish that route before running a campaign. myfoodlicense.com offers complete claims review and substantiation-dossier preparation.

Natural, fresh, pure and absolute claims

The terms “natural,” “fresh” and “pure” have conditional treatment in the claims rules. Check the actual product and processing. A favourable consumer association with a word is not sufficient grounds to use it. Read the conditional terminology provisions.

Describe the process accurately in the technical brief. Include processing stages, preservation and the role of additives. This gives the reviewer useful facts instead of a marketing explanation such as “made with good ingredients.”

FSSAI's advisory dated 28 May 2025 asks businesses to discontinue “100%” on labels and promotional content because it can misleadingly imply absolute purity or superiority. The advisory is a distinct source of current regulatory guidance. Read the official advisory.

Review every place that uses the affected expression. Product images may be stored in a website media library, seller portal and advertising account. Assign an owner to replace each asset and keep the revised versions in one controlled folder.

Comparisons need a defensible reference

Before approving a comparative message, define the reference product and the comparison basis. Keep the original measurements or specifications and the calculation used. A statement chosen first and supported afterwards is more likely to hide an assumption the team has not examined.

Use like-for-like units and understand whether the compared foods and versions fit the applicable rules. Have a reviewer check the chosen wording and reference in the current amended text. Avoid relying on a comparator that no longer exists or on an unexplained industry average.

Hypothetical comparison file

A brand compares two versions of its product but one nutrition table is per serving and the other per 100 g. Its first task is to align the data basis. Only then can the team calculate and review the proposed statement. The illustration does not approve any percentage claim.

Build a claims file before approving artwork

Use one record per claim. Keep the exact wording, approved product version, evidence sources, assessment, conditions of use and review date. Add any requirement to revisit the decision when evidence or the product changes.

  • Identify who owns the recipe and product specifications.
  • Record the claim type and the applicable source provision.
  • Retain relevant reports and any checked calculations.
  • Document what the claim assessment assumes and excludes.
  • Store the approved wording with the final artwork and digital copy.
  • Set a trigger for reassessment after formulation, supplier or audience changes.

Download the claim-review worksheet

Keep websites, listings and campaigns consistent

Make an asset register for the pack, website, marketplaces, advertisements and promotional scripts. Assign the approved wording to each asset. Before launch, check whether anyone has shortened the phrase in a way that changes its meaning.

A claim can drift when a sales team turns a qualified statement into a short headline or a creator improvises a stronger benefit. Give everyone the approved wording and the evidence-based boundaries. Review revised scripts and customer-facing assets before they are used.

Connect this process with the label review and product classification. A claim assessment is strongest when the reviewer knows exactly which food, category and consumer communication are being considered.

Explore the detailed guides

Use these focused articles to work through the decisions relevant to your business.

  • Can You Call Your Food "Natural", "Fresh", "Pure" or "Original"?
  • "High Protein", "Low Fat", "Sugar Free": Criteria for Nutrition Claims
  • Nutrition Claims vs Health Claims: The Difference and Why It Matters
  • "No Added Sugar" vs "Sugar Free" vs "Zero Sugar"
  • "Immunity Booster" and Other Risky Claims Brands Still Make
  • Influencer Marketing for Food Brands: The Rules on Claims
  • Comparative Claims ("30% Less Sugar"): How to Make Them Safely
  • Misleading Food Ads: Penalties and Real Examples
  • Do You Need Evidence for Your Claim? Building a Substantiation File

posts.title: Can You Call Your Food "Natural", "Fresh", "Pure" or "Original"?
posts.description: Natural, fresh, pure and original are regulated food representations, not unrestricted marketing adjectives
posts.lede: Natural, fresh, pure and original are regulated food representations, not unrestricted marketing adjectives. Assess the complete food, processing and consumer impression against the Advertising and Claims rules. Putting the word into a brand name does not automatically avoid the assessment.
posts.body:
Identify what the word describes

Record whether the term describes the entire product, an ingredient, the process or a brand. A claim that one ingredient is natural does not automatically justify natural food for the complete recipe. Read the wording together with photographs, headlines and surrounding copy.

Apply Schedule V to the actual facts

The claims regulations set conditions for terms such as natural, fresh, pure, traditional and original. Processing and composition matter, and a multi-ingredient product needs a different review from a single ingredient. Check the exact term rather than treating the words as synonyms. Read Schedule V.

Review brand-name disclaimers

Where a trademark, brand or fancy name containing the listed adjectives is likely to mislead about the food’s nature, the regulation specifies a prominent disclaimer. It also prescribes minimum font sizes by principal-display-panel area. A trademark registration alone does not establish exemption from food-claim duties.

Check the 100% advisory separately

FSSAI’s May 2025 advisory asks businesses to discontinue 100% representations on labels and promotional material because of their misleading potential and lack of a defined regulatory basis. Identify it accurately as an advisory and assess the complete wording. Read the official advisory.

Build evidence before campaign approval

Keep ingredient specifications, process description, exact wording and the reason it meets the applicable condition. Review website, marketplace and influencer versions as well as the pack. Where a term cannot be supported, rewrite the message around accurate factual attributes rather than changing only its punctuation.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A mixed snack contains minimally processed nuts but also a sweetened coating and flavour blend. The review does not extend the nuts’ natural description to the entire recipe automatically. It examines the proposed full-product wording and the processing evidence.

Your practical checklist

  • Record the exact adjective and subject.
  • Review complete formulation and processing.
  • Apply the term-specific conditions.
  • Assess misleading brand-name wording.
  • Review 100% representations separately.
  • Approve consistent copy across channels.

faq.a: Not automatically. Review the complete product and message.

faq.a: No. Food representations and relevant disclaimers still need assessment.

faq.a: Check the relevant processing and presentation conditions.

faq.q: Where should I keep supporting evidence?

posts.title: "High Protein", "Low Fat", "Sugar Free": Criteria for Nutrition Claims
posts.description: Nutrition claims must meet the Indian criterion for the exact nutrient, food form and reporting basis
posts.lede: Nutrition claims must meet the Indian criterion for the exact nutrient, food form and reporting basis. Sugar-free and low-fat use defined concentration limits, while high-protein uses specified RDA-based alternatives. Do not copy a foreign claim threshold onto an Indian label.
posts.body:
Start with a claim-specific test

Identify the precise wording, product form, serving and category. The criteria for a conventional food and specialised supplement can differ. Check both the claim rule and the product’s own category requirements. Read Schedule I and related notes.

Common concentration thresholds

ClaimSolid foodLiquid food
Sugar-freeNot more than 0.5 g sugars per 100 gNot more than 0.5 g sugars per 100 ml
Low sugarNot more than 5 g per 100 gNot more than 2.5 g per 100 ml
Low fatNot more than 3 g fat per 100 gNot more than 1.5 g fat per 100 ml
Fat-freeNot more than 0.5 g per 100 gNot more than 0.5 g per 100 ml

Apply the exact criterion and qualifications, rather than rounding a borderline analytical value down to fit the claim.

High protein has an Indian RDA basis

The cited high/rich protein criterion provides alternatives: 20% RDA per 100 g of solid food, 10% per 100 ml of liquid food, 10% per 100 kcal or 20% per serving. These are not a universal rule that 20% of energy must come from protein. Record the selected permissible basis and reference value before calculating.

Evidence must reflect the sold product

Review the current recipe, appropriate test evidence, manufacturing variation and shelf-life behaviour. Check whether preparation changes the reporting basis. A supplier’s protein percentage does not establish the finished snack’s claim, and a small serving should not be chosen solely to manipulate presentation.

Align label and advertising

Declare claimed nutrients as required and use consistent wording on the pack and online. A compliant concentration claim does not authorise a disease or therapeutic message. Keep the calculation, reports and approved copy in the file. Distinguish nutrition and health claims.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A beverage contains 0.8 g sugars per 100 ml. It does not meet the cited sugar-free concentration limit, even if a tiny serving provides very little sugar. The team reviews alternative accurate wording instead of treating zero added sugar as evidence of sugar-free status.

Your practical checklist

  • Identify exact claim and food category.
  • Select the correct form and criterion.
  • Record units and any RDA basis.
  • Use current finished-product evidence.
  • Review borderline values and variation.
  • Align declarations and advertising.

faq.a: The cited Indian criterion uses specified RDA-based alternatives; do not substitute a foreign energy rule.

faq.q: Can low sugar mean sugar-free?
faq.a: No. The concentration criteria differ.

faq.q: Does no added sugar prove sugar-free?
faq.a: No. Naturally present sugars still count for the sugar-free concentration assessment.

faq.q: Can I use a raw-material report?
faq.a: It is supporting input evidence, not a complete finished-product claim assessment.

faq.q: Do supplement claims use the same table automatically?
faq.a: No. Check the specialised category and relevant regulatory notes.

posts.title: Nutrition Claims vs Health Claims: The Difference and Why It Matters
posts.description: A nutrition claim describes a nutrient level or comparison; a health claim links a food or constituent to health
posts.lede: A nutrition claim describes a nutrient level or comparison; a health claim links a food or constituent to health. The distinction changes the criteria and evidence needed. Neither category should be used to present an ordinary food as a treatment for disease.
posts.body:
Classify the sentence, not just the headline

Example wordingQuestion to assess
High in proteinDoes it meet the applicable nutrient-content criterion?
Less sugar than the reference foodDoes the comparison meet the relevant conditions?
A statement about normal physiological functionDoes it fit an allowed health-claim route and supporting evidence?
Treats diabetesDoes it improperly represent a food as treating disease?

These are classification prompts, not approved claims for a particular product. Read the claim definitions.

Review the full consumer impression

A pack can imply a benefit through pictures, product names and testimonials even when the nutrient statement is accurate. Examine the complete label, website and campaign together. Removing one verb does not necessarily remove a therapeutic implication.

Choose the appropriate evidence

A concentration claim needs suitable product data and the criterion calculation. A function or health claim can require scientific evidence relevant to the substance, dose, food and intended population. Product-led claims and claims requiring prior approval need their specific route. Current approval-submission framework.

Keep conditions with the wording

Where a permitted claim has conditions of use, population or qualifying information, preserve them in the approved-copy record. Do not shorten an assessed sentence until its necessary context disappears. Advertising space limits are a design constraint, not a reason to discard regulatory conditions.

Control all variants

Maintain a claims register showing category, exact wording, source, evidence and status. Give designers and marketing teams the approved versions. A nutrition claim used on the pack should not become a disease promise in an influencer script. Review influencer communication.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A cereal brand can support a qualifying protein content statement but proposes a campaign promising immunity against infection. The second representation introduces a health and therapeutic assessment that the nutrient calculation alone cannot resolve.

Your practical checklist

  • Record the full proposed sentence.
  • Classify content, comparison or health representation.
  • Assess the complete consumer impression.
  • Match evidence to the claim route.
  • Preserve required conditions and context.
  • Control approved wording across channels.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Health Claim Review service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

headings.text: Classify the sentence, not just the headline

faq.q: Is high protein a health claim?
faq.a: It is ordinarily a nutrient-content claim, subject to the applicable criterion.

faq.q: Can images create a claim?
faq.a: Yes. Review the overall presentation and implied message.

faq.q: Does a lab report support every health claim?
faq.a: No. The evidence must match the specific claimed effect and conditions.

faq.q: Can a food claim to cure disease?
faq.a: Ordinary food representations must not become prohibited treatment or cure claims.

faq.q: Do some claims need prior approval?
faq.a: Yes. Assess the specific route and current ePAAS submission requirements.

posts.title: "No Added Sugar" vs "Sugar Free" vs "Zero Sugar"
posts.description: No added sugar concerns how a food is formulated; sugar-free concerns its final sugar concentration
posts.lede: No added sugar concerns how a food is formulated; sugar-free concerns its final sugar concentration. A food can contain naturally present sugars and still need a non-addition assessment, while failing the sugar-free limit. Zero sugar should not be treated as an unrestricted alternative phrase.
posts.body:
Apply separate tests

For sugar-free, the cited Schedule I limit is not more than 0.5 g sugars per 100 g or 100 ml. For no added sugar, examine ingredients and processing against the non-addition conditions. A nutrition report and a recipe review answer different parts of the question. Read sugar and non-addition criteria.

Check indirect sugar sources

The non-addition rules address sugar-containing components and ingredients used as substitutes for added sugars, including relevant fruit concentrates or pastes. Honey, sweetened fillings or similar inputs cannot be ignored merely because no bag of sucrose enters the factory.

Consider naturally present sugar

Where the food contains naturally occurring sugars, the applicable accompanying statement must be reviewed. The total-sugars figure should accurately reflect the final product. Do not imply that natural origin makes those sugars disappear from the nutrition or sugar-free assessment.

Review processing and sweeteners

Assess whether the process increases sugar content through the situations addressed by the regulation. A non-sugar sweetener can create its own permission and declaration questions. Removing added sugar does not automatically establish that every substitute is permitted or that the food is healthier.

Use evidence and wording consistently

Retain ingredient specifications, formula, process details, analytical evidence and the approved message. Check product title, pack, listing and influencer copy. No added sugar on the pack should not become contains no sugar on the website. Build the claim file.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A fruit bar uses date paste to sweeten the recipe and proposes no added sugar because it contains no refined sucrose. The review examines the paste’s role under the non-addition conditions and the final sugar concentration. Neither proposed sugar claim follows simply from avoiding table sugar.

Your practical checklist

  • Separate concentration and non-addition assessments.
  • Review all sugar-containing components.
  • Identify ingredients used as sugar substitutes.
  • Check naturally occurring-sugar wording.
  • Assess processing and sweetener permissions.
  • Align every channel with approved copy.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Nutrition Claim Review service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

faq.q: Can a no-added-sugar food contain sugar?
faq.a: Yes. Naturally present sugars can remain, subject to the applicable conditions and accompanying statement.

faq.q: Does honey avoid the added-sugar assessment?
faq.a: No. Review the full formula and non-addition conditions.

faq.q: Is zero sugar a free marketing phrase?
faq.a: No. Assess its consumer meaning and applicable sugar-claim criteria.

faq.q: Can a sweetener be used without other checks?
faq.a: No. Permission and label requirements remain separate.

faq.q: Can a test alone prove no added sugar?
faq.a: No. The recipe and processing evidence are also necessary.

posts.title: "Immunity Booster" and Other Risky Claims Brands Still Make
posts.description: Immunity booster is a health representation that needs a precise regulatory and evidence assessment
posts.lede: Immunity booster is a health representation that needs a precise regulatory and evidence assessment. A permitted vitamin or botanical does not automatically authorise a broad immunity promise. Claims implying prevention, treatment or cure of disease are especially problematic for food products.
posts.body:
Translate the phrase into a testable claim

Write what the consumer is being told will happen, for whom and at what dose. Broad words such as protects, prevents infections or boosts defence can imply different effects. Review images, medical references and testimonials alongside the headline.

Separate nutrient function from disease protection

A statement about an established normal nutrient function is not interchangeable with a promise of immunity against illness. Apply the allowed-claim conditions and relevant evidence to the exact wording. Do not extend a general nutrient role to a quantified reduction in infections. Read health-claim provisions.

Check product and dose relevance

Review the finished product, recommended usage, nutrient or ingredient amounts and stability. An ingredient study at a different dose or on another population may not support the proposed food claim. A blend’s branding is not evidence that the complete product has the claimed effect.

Identify approval requirements

Some claims require prior approval or a specific notification route. The 2026 ePAAS order includes relevant claims and product approvals in its single-window framework. Establish the applicable route before relying on a filed dossier as permission to advertise. Read the current order.

Review vulnerable audiences and campaigns

Claims aimed at children, pregnant consumers or people managing disease need an especially careful category and evidence assessment. Give marketing partners controlled wording and review translations. A not-for-medicinal-use disclaimer does not repair a contradictory disease promise. Read supplement claims.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A vitamin drink proposes prevents seasonal infections after its supplier shares a general review article. The brand assesses the exact dose and claim, rejects the leap from nutrient function to disease prevention and prepares a supported wording decision before campaign design.

Your practical checklist

  • Define the claimed effect precisely.
  • Review implied disease representations.
  • Check product, dose and population relevance.
  • Assess evidence quality and applicability.
  • Identify any approval or notification route.
  • Control translations and campaign versions.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Health Claim Review service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

headings.text: Translate the phrase into a testable claim
Separate nutrient function from disease protection

faq.q: Is immunity booster automatically allowed?
faq.a: No. It needs a claim-specific regulatory and evidence assessment.

faq.q: Does a vitamin make the claim valid?
faq.a: Not by itself. Product amounts, wording and conditions matter.

faq.q: Can a disclaimer fix a cure promise?
faq.a: No. Review the complete contradictory impression.

faq.q: Do ingredient studies prove a blended product claim?
faq.a: Not automatically. Establish relevance to the product and claimed use.

faq.q: Are children’s claims assessed differently?
faq.a: Age, product category and evidence relevance can materially affect the assessment.

posts.title: Influencer Marketing for Food Brands: The Rules on Claims
posts.description: Food claims remain subject to the applicable rules when delivered by an influencer
posts.lede: Food claims remain subject to the applicable rules when delivered by an influencer. Paid or other material connections also need appropriate disclosure under the relevant advertising framework. A testimonial cannot establish a health effect that the brand’s product evidence does not support.
posts.body:
Map the campaign relationship

Record payment, free products, affiliate commissions and other material connections. Identify the brand, agency, influencer and approval owner. A campaign agreement should define who checks disclosure and claim wording before content is posted.

Review statutory food claims first

Apply the Advertising and Claims rules to spoken words, captions, visuals, product names and implied benefits. An influencer saying it is my experience does not remove the claim assessment. Avoid treatment or cure messages and unsupported before-and-after representations. Read food advertising requirements.

Apply disclosure guidance accurately

ASCI’s influencer guidance addresses material-connection disclosures and how they are presented. It also includes specialist requirements for health advice and qualification disclosure. Identify ASCI as a self-regulatory body; its guidance supplements rather than replaces statutory food and consumer-protection duties. Read ASCI influencer guidelines.

Give creators a controlled brief

Supply approved statements, necessary conditions, prohibited extensions, disclosure requirements and the evidence contact. Explain that improvised claims and translations need review. Short video, live sessions and stories all need a plan for visible or audible information appropriate to the format.

Monitor and correct the published content

Archive the final post and monitor changes, captions and reused clips. Establish a process to correct inaccurate material promptly and preserve the decision record. Deleting a campaign internally does not ensure that an agency, affiliate or reposted clip stops making the same claim.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A creator changes high protein in the approved brief to cures weakness in the recording. The brand’s review catches the new therapeutic implication before posting. The product’s nutrition evidence does not authorise that improvised sentence, even with a sponsorship label.

Your practical checklist

  • Record material connections and responsibilities.
  • Review words, images and implied benefits.
  • Apply appropriate disclosures.
  • Assess health-credential guidance where relevant.
  • Provide controlled approved copy.
  • Archive and monitor the published versions.

posts.title: Comparative Claims ("30% Less Sugar"): How to Make Them Safely
posts.description: A less sugar or more protein statement needs a valid reference food, a transparent comparison and the applicable difference criterion
posts.lede: A less sugar or more protein statement needs a valid reference food, a transparent comparison and the applicable difference criterion. A large percentage on the pack is not sufficient. Preserve the reference identity, product data and calculation used to support the comparison.
posts.body:
Choose a meaningful reference

Compare foods that meet the applicable comparable-food conditions and use the same quantity basis. Define the reference clearly enough for the claim to be understood. Comparing a prepared product with an unrelated dry concentrate can create a misleading result. Read comparative-claim conditions.

Apply the correct difference rule

The cited rules generally require at least a 30% relative difference for energy or macronutrients, with specified sodium and micronutrient treatment. Sodium uses a 25% difference criterion; micronutrient comparison has a 10% RDA absolute-difference assessment. Read qualifications for the exact claim rather than applying 30% to everything.

Show the calculation

For a hypothetical reference containing 10 g sugar per 100 g and a new product containing 7 g, the relative reduction is (10 − 7) ÷ 10 × 100 = 30%. This calculation demonstrates the percentage only. Reference suitability, evidence, minimum differences and presentation still require review.

Use current and representative evidence

Record the test or other justified data, recipe versions and sampling basis for both products. If the reference or new formula changes, reassess the claim. One historical result from a discontinued reference product should not silently support a current campaign.

Explain the comparison consistently

Keep reference and relevant difference information with the claim as required. Review prominent headlines and qualifiers together. A qualifying comparative claim does not establish that the food is low in sugar, low in fat or healthier overall; those are separate representations. Read nutrient-content criteria.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A snack reduces sugar from 20 g to 14 g per 100 g. It assesses a 30% reduction claim against the appropriate reference, while recognising that the product does not thereby meet the cited low-sugar limit. Relative improvement and an absolute content claim answer different questions.

Your practical checklist

  • Define the valid reference food.
  • Use matching quantity and preparation bases.
  • Select the nutrient-specific difference rule.
  • Keep evidence for both products.
  • Record the percentage calculation.
  • Review qualifiers and separate health implications.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Comparative Claim Review service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

faq.q: Does 30% less automatically mean low sugar?
faq.a: No. Low-sugar criteria are separate.

faq.q: Can I compare unrelated food formats?
faq.a: Assess the applicable comparable-food conditions and avoid a misleading basis.

faq.q: Is every comparison subject to 30%?
faq.a: No. Sodium and micronutrients have specific treatment.

faq.q: Should I name the reference?
faq.a: Provide the reference and difference information required for the claim.

faq.q: Does reformulation affect existing comparison claims?
faq.a: Yes. Recheck the evidence and calculation after relevant changes.

posts.title: Misleading Food Ads: Penalties and Real Examples
posts.description: Misleading food advertising can create liability under section 53 of the Food Safety and Standards Act and other applicable frameworks
posts.lede: Misleading food advertising can create liability under section 53 of the Food Safety and Standards Act and other applicable frameworks. The section states a penalty up to ₹10 lakh for its defined conduct. Actual liability depends on the advertisement, evidence and legal process.
posts.body:
Review express and implied messages

The Act addresses advertising that misleads or deceives about food and false guarantees, with its stated scope. Product names, pictures and testimonials can matter alongside the sentence in small print. A disclaimer cannot be assumed to neutralise a contradictory dominant message. Read section 53.

A documented example: 100% representations

FSSAI’s 28 May 2025 advisory asks food businesses to discontinue use of 100% on labels and promotional material. The authority explains the misleading potential and absence of a defined regulatory basis. This is a real official advisory, not a claim that a particular company was convicted or fined. Read the advisory.

A regulatory example: natural brand wording

The claims regulations specify a disclaimer where listed adjectives in a brand, trademark or fancy name are likely to mislead about the food’s nature. This is a concrete regulatory response to a type of misleading representation. It does not establish that every brand containing such a word has committed an offence. Read the brand-name provision.

Distinguish statutory maxima from case outcomes

Do not present the section 53 maximum as the fine imposed in every case. Misbranding and unsafe-food provisions are separate. Where an actual notice arrives, identify the grounds, channels, versions and period concerned, preserve evidence and obtain advice on the response. Read notice handling.

Build a prevention and correction system

Approve exact wording against the product file, control campaign variants and monitor published material. Where an error is identified, assess removal, correction and affected stock or channels promptly. Keep a record of the assessment and action; a private instruction to an agency is not proof that every advertisement has changed.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A brand’s compliant no-added-sugar pack is advertised online as completely sugar-free. The campaign review identifies a distinct concentration claim lacking support. It corrects the channel wording and preserves the evidence record instead of relying on the pack’s different statement.

Your practical checklist

  • Archive the exact advertisement and channel.
  • Review express and implied claims.
  • Match wording to evidence and criteria.
  • Distinguish advisory, allegation and adjudicated outcome.
  • Assess actual notices and deadlines separately.
  • Document corrections across all affected channels.

posts.title: Do You Need Evidence for Your Claim? Building a Substantiation File
posts.description: A claim-substantiation file should connect the exact proposed wording to the applicable criterion and relevant product evidence
posts.lede: A claim-substantiation file should connect the exact proposed wording to the applicable criterion and relevant product evidence. It is a decision record, not a collection of favourable articles. Keep approved wording, conditions and unresolved issues visible for every SKU and channel.
posts.body:
Record the claim precisely

List the product, recipe version, audience, dose or serving, exact wording, translations and channels. Include images and implied messages where they affect meaning. A file for supports normal function should not silently authorise prevents illness in a later campaign.

Map the regulatory basis

Classify the claim as content, comparative, non-addition or health-related and identify its applicable provisions. Record any prior-approval or notification requirement. The 2026 ePAAS order is relevant where the approval route applies. Claims framework; current approval channel.

Assemble evidence with relevance checks

For nutrient claims, keep the formula, reports, units and criterion calculation. For comparative claims, include the reference evidence. For health claims, examine study quality, population, substance, dose, finished-product relevance and outcome. A supplier brochure is not equivalent to a suitable scientific substantiation.

Document the assessment

Explain why the evidence supports the exact sentence and identify limitations. Record conditions of use, mandatory accompanying wording and the review decision. If evidence does not establish the claim, mark it unresolved or revise the message rather than hiding the gap in a long bibliography.

Control approval and refresh triggers

Give teams a register of approved versions and conditions. Reopen the file after formula, supplier, dose, audience or legal changes. Monitor shelf-life evidence where nutrient content is material to the claim. Retain superseded versions so previous campaigns remain traceable.

A worked example

Hypothetical example

A protein snack’s file contains a raw-material certificate but no finished-product calculation. The reviewer adds the recipe and relevant product data, checks the Indian claim criterion and records the selected basis. Marketing receives the approved wording rather than the entire unfiltered research folder.

Your practical checklist

  • Record exact wording, SKU and channels.
  • Identify criterion and approval route.
  • Assess evidence relevance and quality.
  • Keep calculations and reference products.
  • Record conditions and the decision.
  • Define change and refresh triggers.

Download this preparation checklist

For help applying this review to your business, explore our Claims Substantiation Dossier service. Bring the documents described above so the consultation can focus on the decisions still unresolved.

faq.q: Is a supplier brochure enough?
faq.a: Usually it is input information, not a complete product-specific substantiation.

faq.q: Do all claims need the same evidence?
faq.a: No. Evidence must fit the claim type and applicable rule.

faq.q: Should rejected wording be kept?
faq.a: Retain the decision history so unsupported versions are not reused accidentally.

faq.q: When should a file be refreshed?
faq.a: After relevant formula, supplier, dose, audience, evidence or regulatory changes.

faq.q: Does a large bibliography guarantee approval?
faq.a: No. Relevance, quality and the applicable route matter.
